title: Giving things to people
description: Say who you give something to, and who you take it from.
grammarNote: The indirect object comes before the verb: le doy el libro. It answers a quién.

explanation.summary: Some verbs give something to someone: dar, entregar, enviar, enseñar, traer. The person is an indirect object, and it comes before the verb, with a pronoun for it: le doy el libro, a ella le doy el libro.

sections.heading: The eight pronouns
sections.body: Me, te, se, nos, os, les. They replace the person, and they go before the verb. Se is used when the person is not named, or when it is third person and you do not want to say who: se lo doy. The form le and les are used for a male and a female person, so there is no distinction in the pronoun itself.

examples.en: Can you give it to me?

sections.heading: With dar, it can also mean to take away
sections.body: Dar has a second use: quitar. Darle a alguien un paseo means to take someone for a walk. This is the one place where the indirect object can come after the verb, because the whole phrase is a set expression.

examples.es: Darle a Pedro un paseo por el parque.
examples.en: To take Pedro for a walk in the park.

items.note: To me. It goes before the verb: me lo das.
To you. It goes before the verb: te lo doy.
To him, her or them, when the person is not named.
To us. It goes before the verb: nos lo das.
To them. It is used for a male or a female person.
An infinitive ending in -ar: entrego, entregas, entrega.
An infinitive ending in -ar: envío, envías, envía. The yo form drops the e.
An infinitive: traigo, traes, trae. The yo form is irregular.
Masculine: el regalo. It also means to give.

drills.note: The indirect object comes before the verb.

drills.meaning: can you give it to me?
